text: With the last piece of bread. <break time="0.8s" /> Tom King wiped his plate clean. <break time="0.8s" /> Of the last drop of flour gravy. <break time="0.8s" /> And then he chewed the mouthful slowly. <break time="0.8s" /> The flour for the gravy. <break time="0.8s" /> Had been borrowed from a neighbor. <break time="0.8s" /> And the last two halfpennies in the house. <break time="0.8s" /> Had gone to buy the bread. <break time="0.8s" /> The children had been sent to bed early. <break time="0.8s" /> So that they might sleep. <break time="0.8s" /> Through the missing supper. <break time="0.8s" /> And his wife, Lizzie. <break time="0.8s" /> Had eaten nothing at all. <break time="0.8s" /> He looked every inch a fighter. <break time="0.8s" /> With a flattened nose, a swollen ear. <break time="0.8s" /> A heavy jaw. <break time="0.8s" /> And sleepy, lion like eyes under heavy lids. <break time="0.8s" /> Yet he was not a cruel man. <break time="0.8s" /> And outside the ring. <break time="0.8s" /> He had never once picked a quarrel. <break time="0.8s" /> For to him fighting was simply a business. <break time="0.8s" /> He looked down at his hands. <break time="0.8s" /> At the swollen veins and the battered knuckles. <break time="0.8s" /> And he knew. <break time="0.8s" /> That his body was growing old and tired. <break time="0.8s" /> I wish I had a piece of steak, he said. <break time="0.8s" /> And Lizzie told him. <break time="0.8s" /> That both butchers had refused. <break time="0.8s" /> To give them any more credit. <break time="0.8s" /> Burke the butcher had even said. <break time="0.8s" /> That Sandel would probably beat him that night. <break time="0.8s" /> Though in the old days. <break time="0.8s" /> Burke would have trusted him. <break time="0.8s" /> With a thousand steaks.
